summary: Clarify aggregate tenant quota behavior for subaccounts and why concurrent subkey requests return 429s
description: Issue summary: Customer reports unexpected 429 throttles across multiple API keys belonging to the same top-level tenant and subaccounts during a scheduled backfill and real-time traffic spike. Impact: Production ingestion jobs intermittently fail with 429s, downstream feature extraction jobs delayed ~20-40 minutes, and customer reported potential SLA breach. Environment: prod, us-east-1, multiple API keys created under a single org with two subaccounts (ingest, realtime). Observed behavior: During a coordinated backfill (500 parallel workers) + burst of realtime chat sessions, several short-lived API keys and long-lived keys saw immediate 429 responses despite per-key quotas appearing available in Console. Expected behavior: Per-key quotas should allow parallel usage up to configured per-key limits when tenant-level aggregate is not exhausted.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Create a top-level tenant with two subaccounts and generate 4 API keys (2 long-lived, 2 ephemeral).
2) Start a backfill with 500 parallel workers issuing embedding batches (batch size 32) spread across 2 long-lived keys.
3) Simultaneously start 200 short-lived chat sessions using ephemeral keys that are rotated every minute.
4) Observe 429s beginning at T+30s of the spike and continuing for several minutes even though per-key dashboards show token buckets not fully depleted.
investigation_notes: 2026-03-10 10:24 - Initial triage by Support: verified 429s and captured sample request IDs (req_4a7f...).

2026-03-10 10:40 - SRE pulled rate-limiter metrics: tenant aggregate token bucket drained rapidly due to high concurrency from both backfill workers and many ephemeral key creations. Per-key buckets were not the limiting factor; tenant-level bucket was the bottleneck.

2026-03-10 11:05 - Hypothesis: ephemeral keys cause per-key warmups + health-check probes from the ingestion library to increment tenant-level counters (health probe stamps), accelerating aggregate consumption and creating 'invisible' accounting that isn't shown in per-key Console views.

2026-03-10 11:35 - Reproduced in staging with synthetic traffic: rotating ephemeral keys at 1-min TTL + 300 parallel workers consumed tenant burst tokens much faster than anticipated and caused 429s for stable keys despite their visible buckets being non-empty.

2026-03-10 11:50 - Observed TTL collision: ephemeral key issuance triggered short connection handshakes that are charged at request start (prefix tokens) and do not always surface in per-key token counters due to aggregation windowing in the Console.

root_cause_analysis: Tenant-level aggregate token bucket was exhausted due to a combination of high parallel embedding backfill and many ephemeral key creations that trigger health-check and session-start charge events. The Console displayed per-key counters with slight aggregation lag and did not surface the immediate tenant-level burst accounting, causing a visibility gap.
resolution: Short term: Granted temporary tenant burst quota increase for 4 hours and advised customer to pause ephemeral key rotation during large backfills. Long term: Engineering to (1) make tenant-level accounting visible in Console, (2) adjust health-check accounting to not count lightweight probes toward burst tokens, and (3) publish guidance for ephemeral key patterns and warmup best practices. Customer confirmed recovery.
